essays.stem: A distribution company in Spanish Town is moving its eight sales representatives from office-based work to working mainly on the road and from home. Plan how you would set up the arrangements to lead them well.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by agreeing a written arrangement with each representative, in line with a company policy for offsite work, so that everyone understands the rules. It would set out goals and targets, such as visits, orders and customer satisfaction, and the standards for reports and response times. I would agree core contact hours, a weekly team call and a short daily check-in, and confirm what must be done in writing after calls. I would provide the equipment needed, such as a laptop, phone and secure access to the ordering system, and agree allowances for data and mileage. I would assess the health and safety risks of travel, lone visits and home workstations, and set up a check-in procedure and emergency contacts. I would explain information security rules, such as not storing client data on personal devices. I would arrange training on the tools and make sure each person knows who to call for help. Finally, I would plan regular one-to-one meetings, some team meet-ups, and a review after three months to see what is working and adjust.
markingPoints: Agrees written arrangements, goals and standards in line with policy
Sets a communication rhythm and contact hours
Provides equipment, secure access and allowances
Assesses safety risks and sets up check-ins and security rules
Plans training, one-to-ones, team contact and an early review

essays.stem: Explain how a manager can build trust and team spirit among staff who work in different locations and rarely meet in person.
essays.modelAnswer: Trust grows when people are reliable, open and fair, so the manager should start by keeping her own promises, answering on time and sharing information openly with everyone, not just those in the office. She should agree clear goals and then judge staff by their results rather than by checking on them constantly, because heavy monitoring signals distrust and reduces initiative. Regular one-to-one calls give each person time to raise concerns and feel valued. Team calls should include time for people to share news and successes, not only tasks. The manager can create shared tools, such as a group workspace and a team calendar, so people see each other's work and help each other. Recognising good work publicly and promptly builds pride. Occasional face-to-face meet-ups, such as a quarterly team day, help people form stronger bonds. Offsite staff should be involved in decisions that affect them. When problems arise, the manager should deal with them privately and fairly. Over time, these habits build a team that trusts its leader and each other.
markingPoints: Leads by example with reliability and open information
Manages by results rather than constant checking
Uses one-to-ones and team calls that include social contact
Uses shared tools, recognition and occasional meet-ups
Involves staff in decisions and handles problems fairly

essays.stem: A firm moved 15 claims staff to home working a year ago. Each desk given up saves J$30,000 a month. Each person received equipment costing J$90,000 once and a monthly allowance of J$5,000. Cases handled rose from 1,200 to 1,320 a month, but 60% of the staff say they often feel isolated. Calculate the first-year and later yearly net savings and the change in output, then evaluate the scheme and recommend next steps.
essays.modelAnswer: The yearly saving on desks is 15 × J$30,000 × 12 = J$5,400,000. The equipment cost was 15 × J$90,000 = J$1,350,000, paid once, and the allowances cost 15 × J$5,000 × 12 = J$900,000 a year. The net saving in the first year was J$5,400,000 − J$1,350,000 − J$900,000 = J$3,150,000. In later years, with no new equipment, it is J$5,400,000 − J$900,000 = J$4,500,000, although equipment will need replacing in time. Output rose by 120 cases a month, which is 120 ÷ 1,200 = 10%. On cost and output the scheme is a clear success. However, 60% of the staff feeling isolated is a serious warning: isolation can lead to stress, lower engagement and staff leaving, which would cost more than the savings in recruitment and training. I would recommend keeping the scheme, but using part of the savings to support staff: regular team calls, buddy pairs, a monthly team day in the office, and better access to the employee assistance programme. I would also review the workload behind the higher output and repeat the survey in six months.
markingPoints: Calculates J$5,400,000 desk savings, J$1,350,000 equipment and J$900,000 allowances
Calculates the first-year net saving of J$3,150,000 and J$4,500,000 later
Calculates the 10% rise in output
Evaluates the isolation finding and its risks
Recommends keeping the scheme with specific wellbeing actions and a follow-up review

essays.stem: Explain how a manager should manage the health and safety of offsite staff, such as home-based workers, lone field workers and staff who travel by road.
essays.modelAnswer: The employer's duty of care, and the general duties of the occupational safety and health law, still apply wherever staff work, so the manager must assess the risks for each type of offsite work. For home-based staff, the main risks are poor workstation set-up, long hours at a screen, electrical safety and stress. The manager should give guidance, have each workstation checked, provide a suitable chair and equipment where needed, and encourage breaks and agreed working hours. For lone field workers, such as carers or security officers, the risks include violence, accidents and illness with no one nearby. A check-in system with a clear escalation procedure if a check-in is missed, a charged phone, training in handling difficult situations and the right to leave an unsafe place are key controls. For staff who drive, the risks include crashes, fatigue and robbery, so the firm should check licences and vehicles, plan realistic schedules, ban phone use while driving and set rules for night travel. Staff must know how to report incidents, and the manager should review the arrangements regularly and after any incident.
markingPoints: States that the duty of care applies wherever staff work, in general terms
Covers home-working risks and controls
Covers lone-working risks, check-ins and escalation
Covers road travel risks and controls
Includes incident reporting and regular review

essays.stem: Compare live communication (such as video and phone calls) with written messages that are read later (such as email and shared documents) for leading offsite staff, and recommend how a manager should use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Live communication lets people talk and respond at once. It is best for complex or sensitive matters, such as feedback, bad news, problem solving and building relationships, because tone of voice and expressions help understanding and questions can be answered immediately. Its drawbacks are that people must be free at the same time, which is hard across shifts or time zones, too many calls interrupt focused work, and it leaves no record unless notes are kept. Written messages read later allow people to reply when it suits them, give a clear record and suit routine updates, instructions, reports and sharing documents. Their drawbacks are that messages can be misunderstood, replies may be slow, and long chains of email make information hard to find. I would recommend a planned mix: a weekly team call and regular one-to-one calls for discussion and relationships; a shared workspace and short written updates for routine information; and written confirmation of decisions and instructions after calls. The team should agree which channel to use for what and the expected reply times, so nothing important is lost.
markingPoints: Explains the strengths of live communication and when to use it
Explains its drawbacks
Explains the strengths and drawbacks of written, read-later messages
Recommends a planned mix with examples
Agrees channel rules and reply times with the team

essays.stem: Evaluate how a manager can monitor the performance of offsite staff fairly without intruding on their privacy or damaging trust.
essays.modelAnswer: A manager needs to know whether work is being done well, but cannot see offsite staff working, so she must choose her methods carefully. The fairest approach is to agree clear, measurable goals and standards at the start, such as cases completed, visits made, quality checks passed and customer feedback, and to review them in regular one-to-ones. Shared systems where work is logged, such as job schedules or case management software, give useful information without extra checking. Spot checks of work quality and asking customers for feedback are also reasonable. Tools that track keystrokes, take screenshots or follow staff locations all day are more intrusive. They may be lawful in some cases, but they must have a clear purpose, be explained to staff, be limited to working time and respect the data protection law. Overuse sends a message of distrust, can increase stress and may make good staff leave. On balance, managing by results with open, agreed measures and regular conversation is more effective and fairer. Where tracking is needed, for example for safety on lone visits, it should be explained and kept to that purpose.
markingPoints: Recommends agreed measurable goals and regular reviews
Uses work systems, spot checks and customer feedback
Evaluates intrusive monitoring tools and their effects
Applies privacy and data protection principles in general terms
Reaches a balanced judgement favouring management by results

essays.stem: Explain the information security risks when staff work offsite, and the controls a small firm should put in place.
essays.modelAnswer: Offsite work increases the risk that company and customer information is lost, stolen or seen by the wrong people. Laptops and phones can be stolen from cars or homes, documents can be left in public places, family members may see confidential screens, public Wi-Fi can be insecure, and staff may use personal email or memory sticks to move files. Scam emails are also a greater risk when staff cannot easily check with colleagues. A small firm should have a clear policy for offsite work and train staff on it. Company devices should have passwords, screen locks, up-to-date software and encryption, and be able to be locked or wiped if lost. Staff should reach systems through secure access, such as a VPN, and store files on approved company systems, not personal accounts or devices. Paper records should be kept to a minimum, locked away and shredded when no longer needed. Staff should work where screens cannot be overlooked and avoid discussing client matters in public. Any loss or suspected breach must be reported at once so it can be contained, as the data protection law expects in general terms.
markingPoints: Identifies device theft and loss, and exposure of information
Identifies insecure networks, personal accounts and scam emails
Recommends a policy, training and secured devices
Recommends secure access and approved storage, and care with paper and screens
Requires prompt reporting of breaches

essays.stem: Describe how a manager can recognise and respond to stress and isolation among staff who work from home.
essays.modelAnswer: Because the manager does not see home-based staff every day, she has to watch for signs in other ways. Warning signs include a change in tone in messages, missing meetings, slower or fewer replies, sending emails very late at night, a drop in quality, irritability on calls, or a cheerful person becoming quiet. Regular one-to-one calls, with video if the person is comfortable, give a chance to ask how they are, not only how the work is going. A short, anonymous team survey can show wider patterns. When she notices signs, she should speak privately and calmly, listen without judging and ask what would help. She should look at workload and deadlines, help the person set boundaries on working hours, and encourage breaks and leave. To reduce isolation, she can build regular social contact into team calls, set up buddy pairs and arrange occasional meet-ups. She should point to support such as the employee assistance programme or professional help, and seek urgent help if there is any risk of serious harm. She should follow up, keep the matter confidential and model healthy habits herself.
markingPoints: Identifies warning signs visible at a distance
Uses one-to-ones and surveys to check wellbeing
Responds privately, listens and reviews workload and boundaries
Reduces isolation through contact, buddies and meet-ups
Refers to professional support, urgent help where needed, and follows up confidentially

essays.stem: Plan how you would prepare and facilitate a 60-minute online problem-solving meeting with ten offsite staff from different parishes.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the meeting, I would set a clear purpose, such as finding ways to reduce late deliveries, and send an agenda, the key data and any questions to think about two days ahead. I would choose a time that suits field schedules, check that everyone can use the meeting tool and has a stable connection, and offer a dial-in option for those in areas with weak signal. I would ask one person to keep notes and another to watch the chat. At the start, I would welcome everyone, agree simple ground rules, such as cameras on where possible, one speaker at a time and using the raise-hand button, and confirm the aim. I would share the data briefly, then use short rounds where each person speaks in turn, so quieter or less confident members are heard. Breakout groups of three or four could each work on one cause and report back. I would summarise ideas on a shared screen, help the group choose actions, and agree owners and dates. I would end on time, thank everyone, and send the notes and actions the same day, then follow up at the next meeting.
markingPoints: Sets a purpose and sends the agenda and data in advance
Checks timing, technology and access, including weak-signal options
Agrees ground rules and roles such as note-taker
Uses rounds or breakout groups so all voices are heard
Agrees actions with owners and dates, ends on time and follows up

essays.stem: Explain how a manager should induct and develop new staff who will work mainly offsite, so that they become effective and stay with the firm.
essays.modelAnswer: New offsite staff can feel lost quickly, so induction must be planned. Before the first day, the manager should make sure their equipment, system access and allowances are ready. The first days should ideally be spent with the team in person, or at least in planned video sessions, covering the firm's purpose, the role, targets and standards, the policy for offsite work, health and safety, check-in procedures and information security. Training on the systems and tools should be practical, with time to practise. The manager should give the new person a named buddy and a schedule of check-ins, more often at first, such as daily for the first two weeks. Early tasks should be clear and achievable so the person gains confidence, with prompt feedback. For development, the manager should agree a simple plan in the first months, include offsite staff in online training and in stretch tasks or projects, and make sure they are considered fairly for promotion. Regular one-to-ones should cover growth, not just tasks. A review at the end of the probation period checks progress and gives the new person a chance to say what support they still need.
markingPoints: Prepares equipment, access and allowances before the start
Covers role, standards, policy, safety and security in induction
Provides practical training, a buddy and frequent early check-ins
Plans development, online training and fair access to opportunities
Reviews progress at the end of probation

practical1.title: Plan the leadership arrangements for an offsite team
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a made-up case: a Jamaican firm, such as a home care agency, a security company or a sales distributor, is moving a team of 10 to 15 staff to work mainly in the field or from home. The pack describes the team, their work, the locations and the budget. As a group, prepare the leadership arrangements for the team. Each member has a named role: team charter lead (writes a one-page team charter with goals, standards, contact hours, response times and meeting rhythm); communication planner (writes a communication plan showing which channel is used for what, how often and who leads it); safety officer (writes a lone worker and travel safety procedure with a check-in schedule and escalation steps, and a home workstation checklist); security and equipment officer (lists the equipment and allowances needed, with yearly costs in J$ worked out in a spreadsheet and checked twice, and writes five information security rules); and performance lead (sets four to six performance measures based on results, with how they will be reviewed fairly). In a group of four, the team charter lead also writes the communication plan. Every member presents their part to the assessor, who plays the firm's managing director.
materials: Computers with word processing and spreadsheet software
Charter, procedure, checklist and plan templates
Printer, paper, flipchart paper and markers
photos: The lone worker procedure, check-in schedule and workstation checklist
The equipment and allowance spreadsheet on screen, with the security rules
The group presenting to the assessor
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
The charter sets clear goals, standards and contact hours that respect working time
The communication plan matches channels to purposes and includes regular team contact
The safety procedure has a check-in schedule and clear escalation steps
Costs are calculated correctly and were checked twice; security rules are practical
Performance measures are based on results and reviewed fairly
Presented their part clearly and answered the assessor's questions
safety: Treat the case pack as confidential; return it to the assessor
Use made-up staff names only and no real personal information
Plan fair workloads and contact hours that protect staff wellbeing
Share the workload fairly and take a short screen break each hour

practical2.title: Facilitate an online team meeting and a remote one-to-one
practical2.brief: Using a made-up case from the assessor (an offsite team with a problem, such as missed deliveries or late reports), your group runs an online meeting and a remote one-to-one, with members in separate rooms at the Centre using laptops or phones on the Centre's own accounts, and produces the records. Part A (40 minutes): the team meeting. The manager facilitates a problem-solving meeting with an agenda sent in advance, ground rules and a round where everyone speaks; two or three members play offsite staff from role cards (one with a weak connection, one who is quiet); the host and recorder runs the meeting tool, watches the chat, shares the screen and records the actions. Part B (20 minutes): the one-to-one. A different member plays the manager and holds a remote one-to-one with a staff member whose work has slipped and who seems stressed, giving private feedback and agreeing support. Part C (40 minutes): the group writes the meeting notes and action log, a written follow-up to the staff member confirming what was agreed, and a short reflection on what helped and hindered the online meeting. Every member speaks in at least one part and writes at least one document. In a group of four, the host and recorder also plays a staff member in Part A.
materials: Case pack and role cards from the assessor
Laptops or phones with the Centre's video meeting tool and headsets
Agenda, meeting notes, action log and follow-up templates
Separate rooms or quiet areas for each member
photos: The agenda as sent to the team
Screens during the online meeting, showing the shared notes (faces only if all agree)
